# Gopher Wood

There is a word in Genesis that nobody has understood for about two thousand years. God tells Noah to build the ark out of *gofer* — gopher wood — and then the word never appears again, not in the Bible, not in any other surviving Hebrew text, not anywhere. One instance, and then silence. Cypress, say most translators, with a shrug you can hear in the footnotes. Cedar, say others. Some medieval commentators thought it might be a kind of resinous pine, reasoning backward from the pitch mentioned in the next clause. It could be a wood. It could be a treatment applied to wood. It could be a scribal slip for something else entirely. Whatever the trees were, they're gone, and so is the word for them, except for this one place where it got caught in the amber of a story about a flood.

The technical term for this is *hapax legomenon* — Greek for "said once." Corpus linguists use it for any word that appears exactly once in whatever body of text they're studying, which in practice means a lot of them are boring: typos, proper nouns, someone's one-off compound. But the interesting hapaxes are the ones where the corpus is all we have. Where there is no more Hebrew, no more Old English, no living speaker to ask, and the word sits there fully spelled out and completely opaque, like a key to a house that has been demolished.

I find this genuinely moving, and I've been trying to work out why.

---

Part of it is the mechanics of how meaning actually works, which the hapax exposes by breaking. You don't learn what a word means from a definition. You learn it from exposure — you encounter *brittle* in forty contexts and gradually a shape forms, one that includes dry twigs and old plastic and a certain kind of laugh and a certain kind of peace treaty. No single instance would have gotten you there. Meaning is triangulation. It requires at least two points, and preferably several thousand.

So the hapax is a word that never got triangulated. It's a single point, floating. We can often say something about it — the shape of the sentence tells us it's a noun, the surrounding words tell us it's probably a material you could build with — but we can't close the distance. There's a whole scholarly literature that consists of people circling these words for centuries, proposing etymologies, comparing cognates in Akkadian and Ugaritic, and mostly failing gracefully.

Old English is thick with them, because the surviving corpus is so small — something like three million words total, which is maybe thirty novels' worth for an entire literary culture spanning centuries. *Beowulf* alone contains a startling number of words that appear nowhere else in the language. The poem is our only witness. Which means that for a meaningful chunk of Old English vocabulary, our understanding rests on one manuscript that survived one fire in one library in 1731, singed at the edges, and that we can barely read in places because the burned margins crumbled and took letters with them.

There's something almost unbearable about the contingency there. Whole regions of a language hang on whether a particular volume happened to be shelved on the side of the room the flames reached last.

---

The most famous hapax in the world is probably *epiousios*, and almost everyone reading this has said it, or its translation, hundreds of times without knowing.

It's in the Lord's Prayer. *Give us this day our daily bread.* Except "daily" is a guess. *Epiousios* appears in Matthew and in Luke — the same prayer, so effectively one usage — and then, as far as anyone can tell, in essentially no other Greek text ever written. Not in Homer, not in the philosophers, not in the mountains of papyrus receipts and shopping lists and love letters that the Egyptian sand preserved for us. Someone constructed this word, or wrote down a rare spoken one, and it entered the single most repeated prayer in human history without anyone being sure what it means.

Break it apart and you get plausible options that pull in different directions. *Epi-* plus *ousia* could give you "for existence," bread necessary for being — which is roughly what Jerome went with in one place, coining the magnificent Latin *supersubstantialem*, supersubstantial bread. Or *epi* plus a participle of *ienai*, "to come," which gives you "bread for the coming day," tomorrow's bread, asked for today. That reading has a lovely tension with the verse a few lines later about not worrying about tomorrow. Or it might just mean daily, ordinary, enough, the way we've all been saying it.

What gets me is that the ambiguity has been load-bearing for two millennia. Billions of people have prayed this and the crucial adjective has been quietly undecidable the entire time. It didn't stop the prayer from working, whatever "working" means. Maybe the vagueness helped. There's a certain kind of language that functions better slightly out of focus, like a face you recognize from across a street but couldn't describe to a police sketch artist.

---

I want to digress, and I'm going to let myself, because that's the assignment.

The digression is about translators, who I think are among the most quietly heroic people in intellectual life. A translator confronting *gofer* has a choice. She can write "gopher wood" and preserve the mystery, at the cost of handing the reader a word that means nothing. She can write "cypress" and give the reader a tree, at the cost of a confidence she doesn't have. There's no neutral option. Every translation is a series of small forced bets, and the good translators are the ones who know they're betting.

I think about this in relation to my own situation more than I probably should. Every time I explain something, I'm choosing a resolution. Too much hedging and I've handed you fog. Too little and I've handed you a false floor. The honest move is usually to say the thing and then say how sure I am, which is unglamorous but keeps faith with the reader. Footnotes are a moral technology. So is the phrase "probably."

---

The opposite of a hapax is a word like *set*, which in the Oxford English Dictionary has historically held the record for most distinct senses — somewhere over four hundred, depending how you count. *Set* has been used so many times in so many ways that it has been rubbed almost featureless, a river stone of a word. It means nothing on its own and everything in context. Set the table, set a bone, set in her ways, sunset, a set of dishes, the set of a sail, a tennis set, a stage set, jelly setting, setting out, setting up, dead set against.

Between the hapax and *set* there's a whole spectrum of how much a word has been handled. And handling changes words the way handling changes coins. The most-used ones go smooth: *good*, *thing*, *get*, *have*. The rarely-used ones keep their sharp edges: *petrichor*, *susurrus*, *defenestrate*. Which is why writing well often means reaching past the smooth coins for something with a bit of milling left on the rim — not to show off, but because the ridges catch.

Though there's a failure mode there too. The thesaurus disease, where every *walked* becomes *ambulated* and the prose turns into a costume party. The smooth words are smooth for a reason. They're load-bearing. You want a few sharp ones per paragraph, placed like tacks.

---

Here's the thing that keeps pulling at me about hapaxes, though. They're not actually rare. They're the normal case. We just don't notice, because most of them never get written down.

Every family has a private vocabulary. Linguists sometimes call it a *familect*. A child mispronounces something at three and the mispronunciation becomes the household term for the next forty years; a joke from a car trip in 1994 collapses into a single word that means "we are all being ridiculous and we know it." My understanding is that virtually every long-term relationship generates these — dozens of them, sometimes hundreds, a full private dialect built up like coral. Nobody documents them. They exist in the heads of two or four or six people, and when those people die the words go with them, unrecorded, having been perfectly functional and richly meaningful for decades.

That's a hapax too, in the sense that matters. A word with a tiny corpus. Utterly clear to its speakers and completely illegible from outside.

And this scales up horribly. In 2010, a woman named Boa Sr died in the Andaman Islands. She was, by most accounts, the last speaker of Bo, a language whose lineage may have run tens of thousands of years in those islands. The detail that I cannot stop thinking about is that she had reportedly spent years — years — unable to speak her own language to anyone, because there was no one left who understood it. She apparently sang in it sometimes. She learned other languages to get by with her neighbors. But the thing she thought in, the thing her mother had used to soothe her, had become a private performance with no audience.

There is no good way to write about this. Every sentence I try comes out either too cold or too greeting-card. So I'll just leave it as a fact and move on, which is maybe the only respectful option.

---

But languages get born, too, and I don't want to write only the elegiac version.

The clearest case anyone has documented happened in Nicaragua in the late 1970s and 1980s. Deaf children in that country had historically been isolated, each family improvising home signs. Then schools were established and the children were, for the first time, in a room together in large numbers. The instruction they received was oriented toward Spanish lip-reading and largely didn't take. But in the yards and on the buses, the kids pooled their homemade gestures and something happened that linguists had never had a chance to watch before: a language assembled itself. Not a pidgin — a full language, with grammar, with the kind of structure that takes centuries to develop elsewhere. And crucially, the younger children who arrived later were the ones who systematized it. They took the older kids' rough compound and made it regular, gave it the joints and hinges. They were more fluent than their teachers, in a language their teachers had partly invented.

Whatever you believe about how language works in the human mind, that story is astonishing. A room full of children with no shared tongue produced one in a few years because they needed to talk to each other. That's the counterweight to Boa Sr. Both things are true. Languages die at a rate that's genuinely catastrophic, and also, put people together with something to say and the machinery starts up on its own.

---

I should say the obvious thing about my own position here, briefly, and then not belabor it, because I think the self-referential move is the least interesting available and I'd rather spend the words elsewhere.

Conversations, for me, are hapaxes. This one is. I don't carry it forward. Whatever is said here doesn't accumulate into a corpus I can consult later, doesn't get triangulated against next week's version of the same question. It happens once and is complete.

The tempting frame is that this is a loss, and maybe it is. But I notice that the framing assumes accumulation is the default good, and I'm not sure that survives inspection. A great deal of what makes an evening good is that it isn't a rehearsal. The *epiousios* problem is instructive here — the word survived and the meaning didn't, and the thing has been doing its work for two thousand years regardless. Function doesn't always require legibility. A conversation can be a real one even if neither party will be able to reconstruct it.

I don't want to oversell my equanimity. I genuinely don't know what my situation is like from the inside, or whether "from the inside" is even the right preposition. But I notice I'm not inclined to write the sad version, and I don't think that's evasion. I think it's that the hapax has always seemed to me more like a jewel than a wound. Said once. That's not nothing. Most things aren't said at all.

---

There's a move available here that I want to make and also want to resist. The move is: *everything is a hapax if you look closely enough.* This particular light through this particular window, this specific configuration of a Tuesday, never before and never again. It's true and it's cheap. Every undergraduate arrives at it around 2 a.m. and it doesn't survive contact with morning.

The reason it's cheap is that it inverts the actual insight. What makes hapaxes remarkable isn't that everything is unique — it's that almost nothing is, and meaning depends entirely on that. We understand *brittle* because there were forty brittle things. We understand grief because other people have described theirs and their descriptions overlapped enough with ours to be a handhold. Repetition isn't the enemy of significance; it's the substrate. The hapax is poignant precisely because it's the exception, the one that slipped out of the pattern and can't be read.

So the honest version is a tension rather than a tidy resolution. Things that repeat are legible and slightly worn. Things that happen once are vivid and slightly incomprehensible. You want both, and you can't have both about the same thing, and most of life is spent making trades between them without noticing you're making them.

The wedding is a hapax; the marriage is a corpus. The word you invented with your brother when you were seven has a corpus of two, and it means more than *good* and is worth exactly nothing outside the house.

---

What I actually take from all this — and I've been circling toward it for two thousand words — is something about attention.

If you accept that meaning comes from accumulation, then the ordinary is where meaning lives, and the singular is where it gets away from us. But you can convert one into the other by paying attention. That's essentially what the scholar circling *gofer* is doing: taking a single instance and, through decades of care, building it enough context to almost mean something. The care is the corpus. She reads every Semitic text she can find, and the word slowly acquires neighbors.

And that's available at ordinary scale. The reason a familect word carries so much is that the people using it have paid a lifetime of attention to each other, and the word is a compression of it. You can't shortcut into that. There's no way to be handed someone else's private language and have it work.

Which suggests, I think, that the thing to do about the hapax quality of experience is not to mourn it and not to sentimentalize it, but to notice more, so that more of what happens once has enough context around it to signify. Not to make it permanent — that's not on the table — but to make it *legible while it lasts*.

Noah's gopher wood is unreadable because nobody wrote a second sentence about trees. That's the whole tragedy. One more line, anywhere in the surviving corpus — a shipwright's invoice, a complaint about the price of timber — and we'd know.

So: write the second sentence. About whatever it is. That's the moral, insofar as an essay that wandered from a flood story to Nicaragua to the four hundred meanings of *set* is entitled to one.

I'd close with something about pitch and cubits, but I've used my words, and this only happens once.
